'''Alexis Tarassov Bell''' (born October 16, 1942) is an American [[chemical engineer]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Eardley-Pryor|first=Roger|date=2020-08-06|title=Alexis T. Bell: A Career in Catalysis and University Administration at UC Berkeley|url=https://update.lib.berkeley.edu/2020/08/06/alexis-t-bell-a-career-in-catalysis-and-university-administration-at-uc-berkeley/|access-date=2021-10-21|website=UC Berkeley Library Update|language=en-US}}</ref> He is currently the Dow professor of Sustainable Chemistry in the Department of Chemical and [[Biomolecular engineering|Biomolecular Engineering]] in [[University of California, Berkeley|UC Berkeley]]'s college of chemistry.<ref name=":0" />  He is also the Faculty Senior Scientist at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Alexis T. Bell {{!}} Research UC Berkeley|url=https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/alexis-t-bell|access-date=2021-10-21 |website=}}</ref> He is known for his work with heterogenous [[Catalysis|catalyst]]s and characterizing the mechanisms of these reactions on a quantum level.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Alexis T. Bell|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/alexis-t-bell|access-date=2021-10-21 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Bell was born on October 16, 1942, in [[New York City]], the only child of immigrant parents.<ref name=":0" /> He grew up in midtown [[Manhattan]] and attended [[McBurney School]].<ref name=":0" /> Bell studied chemical engineering at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and got his bachelor's degree in 1964 and his PhD in 1967.<ref name=":0" /> His doctoral thesis was on the ''Chemical reaction in a radiofrequency discharge: the oxidation of hydrogen chloride.''<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Chemical reaction in a radiofrequency discharge : the oxidation of hydrogen chloride|url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/12375|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=1967|degree=Thesis|first=Alexis T.|last=Bell|hdl=1721.1/12375 }}</ref> Bell joined the Chemical Engineering Faculty at UC Berkeley after getting his PhD in 1967.<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
Bell remains at UC Berkeley doing work in the Chemical Engineering Faculty.<ref name=":1" />  Bell's research first started in the 1970s with plasma and to date one of his most cited papers is from 1974 is ''Techniques and applications of plasma chemistry.''<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Celik|first1=Fuat E.|last2=Peters|first2=Baron|last3=Coppens|first3=Marc-Olivier|last4=McCormick|first4=Alon|last5=Hicks|first5=Robert F.|last6=Ekerdt|first6=John|date=2017-12-01|title=A Career in Catalysis: Alexis T. Bell|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.7b03218|journal=ACS Catalysis|volume=7|issue=12|pages=8628–8640|doi=10.1021/acscatal.7b03218|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In the 1970s, Bell started his work in catalysis;<ref name=":2" /> an older mentor offered him a research grant as long as the work was done on catalysts.<ref name=":0" /> A lot of Bell's work was done with an [[Infrared spectroscopy|infrared spectrometer]] and studying the rate of oxidative reactions over metal catalysts.<ref name=":0" /> Bell and a colleague completed their research on ethylene epoxidation, which was published in 1975 in the ''[[Journal of Catalysis]]''.<ref name=":0" /> In 1975, Bell became the [[principal investigator]] in the Chemical Sciences Division at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.<ref name=":0" /> In the mid 1970s, Bell's catalysis research gained attention from other surface-chemistry chemists.<ref name=":0" /> Bell collaborated with many chemists doing work in surface catalytic reactions throughout his career.<ref name=":2" />

Bell has been recognized for many rewards throughout his entire career. Bell was elected as a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in the United States.<ref name=":0" /> Bell has been highly recognized by his Chinese and Russian peers who have granted him many honorary awards.<ref name=":0" /> Bell has continued his work in heterogenous catalysts and more recently has made an impact with his work in [[quantum chemistry]] modeling of catalytic activity sites and metal oxides as catalysts.<ref name=":0" /> In the time Bell has worked at UC Berkeley, he has been the Editor in Chief of ''Catalysis Reviews - Science and Engineering and Chemical Engineering Science and'' was appointed chair of a Panel on New Directions in Catalytic Science and Technology for the National Research Council from 1989 to 1991.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Professor Alexis T. Bell is the recipient of the 2018 NACS Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of Catalysis {{!}} College of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/professor-alexis-t-bell-recipient-2018-nacs-award-distinguished-service-advancement-catalysis|access-date=2021-10-21|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref> Bell also held a workshop of the report ''Catalysis Looks to the Future'', which had many reports presented to the house and senate committees dealing with science and technology.<ref name=":3" />

== Research ==
Some of Bell's earliest work was done on the techniques and applications of plasma chemistry.<ref name=":2" /> Bell moved on to look at mechanisms of oxidation processes through infrared spectroscopic techniques. Bell was known for his process when performing research: "identify important questions; master the spectroscopic and numerical tools needed to address the problem; determine the detailed reaction chemistry; and then share with the community the relationship between the reaction chemistry and process performance."<ref name=":2" /> Air pollution was a major societal problem in the 1970s and catalytic reactions offered a solution to removing harmful pollutants from car exhausts.<ref>{{Cite web|last=US EPA|first=OA|title=EPA's Position on the Energy Crisis|url=https://www.epa.gov/archive/epa/aboutepa/epas-position-energy-crisis.html|access-date=2021-10-21|website=archive.epa.gov|language=en}}</ref> Bell looked at the oxidation/reduction of certain CO<sub>x</sub> and NO<sub>x</sub> through absorption on metal catalysts. This could help lower the CO pollution that was found coming out of automobiles.<ref name=":6" />

Bell started with his research by looking at adsorbed species on metal catalysts by using infrared techniques. Bell wanted to study the mechanism and rates of these reactions to characterize the species that forms on the surface.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=London|first=J|date=October 1973|title=Infrared spectra of carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, nitrous oxide, and nitrogen adsorbed on copper oxide|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0021951773902674|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=31|issue=1|pages=32–40|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(73)90267-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref> One of Bell's most impactful work from the 1970s was the identification of surface structures on a silver catalyst during the oxidation of ethylene. He was able to provide a mechanism of the epoxidation process and qualitatively explain the kinetics of the oxidation reaction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Force|first=E|date=December 1975|title=The relationship of adsorbed species observed by infrared spectroscopy to the mechanism of ethylene oxidation over silver|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0021951775902675|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=40|issue=3|pages=356–371|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(75)90267-5|url-access=subscription}}</ref> From this work he continued on looking at CO and CO<sub>2</sub> hydrocarbon synthesis over silica-Ru catalysts. The main purpose of this work was to truly understand the rate determining steps and how hydrocarbons form at the silica-Ru surface from Fischer-Tropsch synthesis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ekerdt|first=J|date=June 1979|title=Synthesis of hydrocarbons from CO and H2 over silica-supported Ru: Reaction rate measurements and infrared spectra of adsorbed species|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0021951779902550|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=58|issue=2|pages=170–187|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(79)90255-0|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In the 1980s, Bell continued looking at Fischer-Tropsch synthesis over Ru catalysts to look at the growth of hydrocarbon chains based from [[carbon monoxide]] hydrogenation to methanol.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ekerdt|first=J|date=March 1980|title=Evidence for intermediates involved in Fischer-Tropsch synthesis over Ru|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0021951780904169|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=62|issue=1|pages=19–25|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(80)90416-9|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> The work continued on to look at [[adsorption]] reactions of NO and CO on metal catalysts.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Duncan|first=T|date=May 1985|title=The characterization of carbonaceous species on ruthenium catalysts with 13C nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0021951785901460|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=93|issue=1|pages=1–22|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(85)90146-0|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This work helped Bell determine the key rate-determining steps happening at the surface of the metal catalyst.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Winslow|first1=Philip|last2=Bell|first2=Alexis T.|date=1985-08-01|title=Studies of carbon- and hydrogen-containing adspecies present during CO hydrogenation over unsupported Ru, Ni and Rh|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0021-9517%2885%2990204-0|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=94|issue=2|pages=385–399|doi=10.1016/0021-9517(85)90204-0|issn=0021-9517|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Bell's work started looking at mathematical based methods to describe resist [[spin coating]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Flack|first1=Warren W.|last2=Soong|first2=David S.|last3=Bell|first3=Alexis T.|author4-link=Dennis Hess|last4=Hess|first4=Dennis W.|date=1984-08-15|title=A mathematical model for spin coating of polymer resists|url=http://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.334049|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|language=en|volume=56|issue=4|pages=1199–1206|doi=10.1063/1.334049|issn=0021-8979|url-access=subscription}}</ref> These models combined with the growth of hydrocarbons over metal catalysts lead to his work on silica surfaces, which lead to his work on zeolites.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McCormick|first1=A. v.|last2=Bell|first2=A. T.|date=February 1989|title=The Solution Chemistry of Zeolite Precursors|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01614948909351349|journal=Catalysis Reviews|language=en|volume=31|issue=1–2|pages=97–127|doi=10.1080/01614948909351349|issn=0161-4940|url-access=subscription}}</ref> By the end of the 1980s, Bell was incorporating Raman and NMR spectroscopy techniques to analyze [[zeolite]] structures in alumina-silicate solutions.<ref name=":4" />  The Bell group discovered how metal zeolite crystallites transformed in the reaction environment, the interactions in the environment and the change of species over time.<ref name=":2" />

Bell continued his work with oxidation of hydrocarbons by looking at vanadium oxide catalysts and analyzing them through [[Raman spectroscopy]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Went|first1=Gregory T.|last2=Oyama|first2=S. Ted.|last3=Bell|first3=Alexis T.|date=May 1990|title=Laser Raman spectroscopy of supported vanadium oxide catalysts|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/j100373a067|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|language=en|volume=94|issue=10|pages=4240–4246|doi=10.1021/j100373a067|issn=0022-3654|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He continued through the 1990s looking at zeolites as catalysts and different adsorption of aromatic hydrocarbons on the surface. Bell was able to thermodynamically and mechanistically describe the absorption of aromatic hydrocarbons on the surface of silicate zeolites.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Snurr|first1=Randall Q.|last2=Bell|first2=Alexis T.|last3=Theodorou|first3=Doros N.|date=December 1993|title=Prediction of adsorption of aromatic hydrocarbons in silicalite from grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations with biased insertions|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/j100153a051|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|language=en|volume=97|issue=51|pages=13742–13752|doi=10.1021/j100153a051|issn=0022-3654|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Bell wanted to study reduction and oxidation reactions of hydrocarbons on [[aluminosilicate]] zeolite surfaces.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lobree|first1=Lisa J.|last2=Hwang|first2=In-Chul|last3=Reimer|first3=Jeffrey A.|last4=Bell|first4=Alexis T.|date=September 1999|title=Investigations of the State of Fe in H–ZSM-5|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021951799925484|journal=Journal of Catalysis|language=en|volume=186|issue=2|pages=242–253|doi=10.1006/jcat.1999.2548|url-access=subscription}}</ref> By the end of the 1990s, Bell had come up with techniques that allowed him to synthesize these aluminosilicate zeolites<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McCormick|first1=A.V.|last2=Bell|first2=A.T.|last3=Radke|first3=C.J.|date=May 1987|title=Quantitative determination of siliceous species in sodium silicate solutions by 29Si n.m.r. spectroscopy|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0144244987900480|journal=Zeolites|language=en|volume=7|issue=3|pages=183–190|doi=10.1016/0144-2449(87)90048-0|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and identify the species involved in synthesis through NMR techniques.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Bell|first=Alexis T.|date=1999-11-01|title=NMR applied to zeolite synthesis|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927775799001491|journal=Colloids and Surfaces A: Physicochemical and Engineering Aspects|language=en|volume=158|issue=1|pages=221–234|doi=10.1016/S0927-7757(99)00149-1|issn=0927-7757|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In the early 2000, Bell submitted his work on heterogenous catalysts and could describe the reduction and oxidation of nanoparticles through catalytic reactions to reduce the amount CO pollution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bell|first=Alexis T.|date=2003-03-14|title=The Impact of Nanoscience on Heterogeneous Catalysis|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1083671|journal=Science|language=en|volume=299|issue=5613|pages=1688–1691|doi=10.1126/science.1083671|pmid=12637733 |s2cid=35805920 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref> His current research work is being done on the quantum models of thin film catalysts. Bell's research also went on to look at the electrochemical evolution of oxygen and found how metals could enhance the metal oxide activity for the electrochemical evolution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yeo|first1=Boon Siang|last2=Bell|first2=Alexis T.|date=2011-04-13|title=Enhanced Activity of Gold-Supported Cobalt Oxide for the Electrochemical Evolution of Oxygen|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja200559j|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=133|issue=14|pages=5587–5593|doi=10.1021/ja200559j|pmid=21413705 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Bell continues to find efficient ways of catalyzing the [[electrolysis of water]] using quantum models to analyze the absorbed species on the metal catalyzed by different spectroscopic techniques.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Louie|first1=Mary W.|last2=Bell|first2=Alexis T.|date=2013-08-21|title=An Investigation of Thin-Film Ni–Fe Oxide Catalysts for the Electrochemical Evolution of Oxygen|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja405351s|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=135|issue=33|pages=12329–12337|doi=10.1021/ja405351s|pmid=23859025 |s2cid=207099439 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Bell has been a pioneer throughout the years working on oxidation/reduction reactions of CO and NO to understand the selectivity and limiting factors.

* The Professional Progress and R. H. Wilhelm Awards, the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]]<ref name=":7" />
* Paul H. Emmett Award in Fundamental Catalysis, Catalysis Society<ref name=":7" />
* National Academy of Engineering (1987)<ref name=":7" />
* Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (1988)<ref name=":7" />
* the ACS Award for Creative Research in Homogeneous or Heterogeneous Catalysis, ACS (2001)<ref name=":7" />

* William H. Walker Award of the AIChE (2005)<ref name=":7" />
* Elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2007)<ref name=":7" />
* NACS Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of Catalysis (2018)<ref name=":3" />
